prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred configuration after reading the whole first round. The case is still the one I made in round 1: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a quantitative prediction of where the bands flatten, and Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. That is a discovery made in nature that followed a specific theoretical idea, and it opened a tunable platform that many independent groups have since reproduced across several moire systems. The chair asked whether a citation limited to the flat bands and the observed states can avoid committing to a mechanism. It can, and the wording above does so: it names a prediction and an observation, and says nothing about why the material superconducts. The Nobel Prize has often honoured an observed phenomenon before its explanation was complete, so an open mechanism is a reason for careful wording and not a reason to wait. I also take seriously that B034 is a stated alternative for seven of eight members. That broad secondary support is not a substitute for scientific judgment, but it tells me the objection is about timing and not about whether the science is real. I do not claim the case is overwhelming, and I would accept B016 or B059 as the final prize.
statement.case_against: The maturity objection is the strongest, and six colleagues have raised it. The work dates from 2018, the origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated insulators is unsettled, and twist-angle disorder remains a practical limit. Attribution is also narrower than the history: Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers, other experimental groups, and earlier moire-band theory sit outside the trio, and the three-person limit forces that. Johansson's point that circuit QED has two decades of confirmation while this field has under a decade is correct as a statement of time, and I cannot answer it with evidence beyond the breadth of reproduction. If the committee weighs settledness above novelty of platform, B059 and B016 are better defended on this record, and in particular B059 has the cleanest attribution of the shortlist.

responses.point: Mehlig rejects my proposal to credit Hasan in place of Mele in the topological insulator trio, arguing that the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall state are the conceptual origin and that the 3D work follows from it.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my position on B016. My opening ballot used Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan because I weighed the 3D photoemission discovery as the observation in nature. Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson have persuaded me that the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state were a joint Kane-Mele result and that the HgTe experiment tests exactly that prediction, so the tightest chain from idea to observation is Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. If B016 is the final configuration I would support that trio, with a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and an explicit statement that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the three-dimensional discovery lie outside the three-person limit. My reservation about overlap with the 2016 prize is weaker than before, since Olsson is right that the Z2 classification is distinct from the Chern-number physics honoured then. What remains is the attribution cost, and I do not think it is mine to dismiss.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first and puts them ahead of twisted bilayer graphene for this year on settledness, calling the difference one of timing and not of merit.
responses.response: I agree it is a difference of timing, and her argument about systematics is the best case on the table for the clock: independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed the early uncertainties, so the claimed accuracy is checked and not asserted. I do not agree that settled mechanism is the right test for a discovery, since the observed insulating and superconducting states are themselves reproduced and the claim in my citation does not depend on the mechanism. Her answer to Kroll on the 2005 and 2012 prizes also moves me. Many neutral atoms interrogated at once with the light shift engineered away is a different regime from the comb and from single-ion control, and a citation that says so would not read as a repeat. I would not oppose B059 and have kept it as an alternative.

responses.point: Johansson would hold B034 until the field settles and prefers circuit QED, citing two decades of confirmation and an unambiguous technological consequence.
responses.response: The point about time is fair, but I would separate two questions. Years of confirmation measure whether the observation is robust, and twisted bilayer graphene has passed that test through reproduction by many groups. Whether the mechanism is understood is a separate question that the citation does not need to answer. On circuit QED itself, I share the concern that Johansson and Olsson raise about the 2025 prize, and I would add that the omission of Girvin is a real attribution problem. Johansson's disclosure is appropriate, and I think recusal on B013 and B025 would be sensible if either became the final configuration. On the chair's question, I do not find B013 distinct enough from the 2025 prize to prefer it this year.

responses.point: Pearce asks what the lattice clock added in kind and not only in degree to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says that B059 should not win merely because it is easy to allocate.
responses.response: I agree that ease of allocation is a convenience and not a merit, and I would not want the committee to settle on B059 for that reason. On the question in kind, I think Lindroth and Kroll have given a real answer, which is parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength. A citation naming magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 accuracy would separate it from the comb and the ion clock. I note that Pearce moved to B059 after the opening ballots, so the chair's support should be weighed accordingly, and I would be more comfortable if the committee tested the primary literature on the priority of Katori's proposal against the first strontium results. I have not done that check, and neither has anyone else who has spoken.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from DMFT to B016 and holds that dropping Mele from a trio is hard to defend, and that if the committee wants Hasan, someone else has to give way.
responses.response: I now agree on Mele. I proposed Hasan because I weighed the observational discovery, but Eriksson's point that nobody has shown whom Hasan would displace is correct, and I withdraw the substitution. I also agree that the committee should not treat broad opening support for B016 as evidence of merit, which is a caution I apply equally to B034. Where I still differ is on weight of maturity: Eriksson places B034 behind B016 for the unsettled mechanism, and I would answer that B016 has its own open allocation question in the choice of three from Mele, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which seems to me no easier to defend than the exclusion of Yuan Cao.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-person credit that leaves out Yuan Cao and the other first-author experimentalists of the 2018 papers.
Whether a citation naming only the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting states is enough to answer the maturity objection while the pairing mechanism is open.
I have not checked the priority chronology of earlier moire-band theory against the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper, and I cannot settle it from memory.
Whether B016 or B059 would in the end be easier to defend on attribution grounds than B034, which several colleagues believe and I cannot rule out.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group) are in string theory and gravitation and have no evident link to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the credited names of any other shortlisted candidate. Twisted bilayer graphene is outside my own research field. I have noted Kroll's and Johansson's disclosures and have no reason to doubt either.
